# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–28 (Complete – Updated 200)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Winter of seventh year after Waterloo**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Continental tour progressing**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin on steamship and carriage tour; landed Rotterdam, traveled to Cologne, now established in Pumpernickel (a small German principality) for autumn/winter season. **Year noted as 1830 (French Revolution occurred this year)**.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate (deed to pastures discovered to be forged by Madrek Orlwood; Feena Stenworth found work there and did not return); Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Staveton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John, Waterloo, Laeken); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Calcutta; Jamaica; Rotterdam; Cologne; Free City of Judenstadt; Rhine region; Rhineland; **Pumpernickel** (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss, Prime Minister's lodgings, Aurelius Platz, Zwieback's Conditorey, Saint Michael's Fountain, Artillery Place, Stadthaus, Town Hall, Redoute, gardens with Trophonius' cave, nymphbath, Niagara cataract); Mirecombe; Dunholt; Dunwick; Quenwick; Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen; Ems; Aix-la-Chapelle; Baden-Baden; Salwick; **Elephant** (lodging-house, Room No. 90/92); Boulogne; Dieppe; Portman Square; Brussels; Paris; Wildbad; Strasburg; St. Petersburg; Toplitz; Vienna; Pincian Hill (Rome); Naples; Castle Gaunt; Trinity House; White Friars; Chiswick; University of Schoppenhausen; Leipzig; Dresden; Schoppenhausen; Clapham.

## Rebecca at Pumpernickel – Gaming and Seduction (Chapters 27–28)

**Arrival and Gaming Encounters**: At Stadthaus gaming, Jos remained at play-table. Woman in foreign accent revealed herself as **Rebecca (Madame de Raudon)**, formerly involved with Rawdon Crawley. Spoke of seeing "dear Amelia," noted she "looked pretty and happy."

**Seduction of Jos (Chapter 28)**: Rebecca in pink domino (faded, soiled) led Jos into garret at Elephant lodging-house (Room No. 92). Hid evidence of degradation (rouge-pot, brandy bottle, plate of broken meat), smoothed hair. Gave tender looks, claimed heart first learned to beat at Jos's presence; denied giving George encouragement; asserted marital duties paramount; promised preserve virtue "to her dying day, or until...Colonel Crawley's...cruelty had rendered odious." Jos departed convinced "that she was the most virtuous, as she was one of the most fascinating of women" and resolved she must quit that place, take quiet lodging, and that Amelia must befriend her.

**Becky's True Nature**: After Jos departed, "Becky bowed Jos out of her little garret with as much grace as if it was a palace of which she did the honours." Max and Fritz (students from Schoppenhausen) came out of hole, pipe in mouth. She mimicked Jos while munching cold bread and sausage and drinking brandy-and-water. **Becky liked the life**: "She was at home with everybody in the place, pedlars, punters, tumblers, students and all. She was of a wild, roving nature, inherited from father and mother, who were both Bohemians, by taste and circumstance." Students reported: Becky advertised concert at Leipzig that did not occur (claimed pianist fell ill at Dresden). She won money at trente-et-quarante using young Georgy to play for her; planned to spend money on wine, theatre, or Cognac in Aurelius Garden rather than buy her own concert tickets.

## Jos and Dobbin's Conflict (Chapter 28)

Jos walked to Dobbin's lodgings with great solemnity and imparted affecting history without mentioning gaming. Two gentlemen consulted as to best means of being useful to Mrs. Becky.

**Major's Distrust and Jos's Resentment**: When Major heard from Jos, excitement was "quite the reverse from a pleasurable one"; he called her "The little minx." Never had slightest liking for her; heartily mistrusted her from first moment when "her green eyes had looked at, and turned away from, his own." Said: "That little devil brings mischief wherever she goes." Questioned who knows what sort of life she has been leading, why abroad and alone, why left husband. Recalled Rawdon was "confounded blackleg" who cheated poor George. Remembered scandal about separation. Jos tried in vain to convince Dobbin that Mrs. Becky was "in all respects a most injured and virtuous female."

Jos became "not a little jealous of the airs of superiority which the Major constantly exhibited towards him" (Jos imparted opinions to Mr. Kirsch, the courier, whose bills Major Dobbin checked on journey, and who sided with Jos). Jos began blustering speech about his competency to defend his own honour, his desire not to have his affairs meddled with, his intention to rebel against the Major. Colloquy—"rather a long and stormy one"—ended simply by arrival of Mrs. Becky with porter from Elephant Hotel in charge of her meagre baggage.

## Amelia's Embrace of Rebecca; Major's Rejection (Chapter 28)

**Becky's Arrival and Greeting**: She greeted Jos with affectionate respect and made shrinking, but amicable salutation to Major Dobbin, who—as her instinct assured her at once—was her enemy and had been speaking against her. Bustle consequent upon her arrival brought Amelia out of her room.

**Amelia's Warmth; Dobbin's Departure**: Emmy embraced her guest with greatest warmth, took no notice of the Major except to fling him "an angry look—the most unjust and scornful glance that had perhaps ever appeared in that poor little woman's face since she was born." She had private reasons of her own and was bent upon being angry with him. Dobbin, indignant at injustice, not defeat, made her a bow quite as haughty as the killing curtsey with which the little woman chose to bid him farewell. He departed.

**Emmy's Bustling Hospitality**: Emmy was particularly lively and affectionate to Rebecca, bustled about apartments and installed her guest with eagerness and activity seldom exhibited by placid little friend. Emmy thought she was displaying great deal of firmness and proper feeling and veneration for late Captain Osborne in her present behaviour. "When an act of injustice is to be done, especially by weak people, it is best that it should be done quickly."

**Becky's False Narrative (Repeated from Prior Consultation)**: Amelia's frankness and kindness touched Becky. She returned Emmy's caresses with "something very like gratitude, and an emotion which, if it was not lasting, for a moment was almost genuine." Becky claimed child "torn from her arms shrieking." Amelia cried out: "Oh, Rebecca, my poor dear suffering friend, I know what it is to lose a boy...But please Heaven yours will be restored to you, as a merciful merciful Providence has brought me back mine."

Becky owned to agonies regarding child "not perhaps without a twinge of conscience. It jarred upon her to be obliged to commence instantly to tell lies in reply to so much confidence and simplicity." Becky gave full version: marriage with Rawdon viewed by family with utmost hostility; sister-in-law (artful woman) poisoned husband's mind against her; he formed odious connections, estranged affections; she bore everything—poverty, neglect, coldness "for the sake of her child"; finally driven to demand separation when wretch asked she sacrifice fair fame for advancement through Marquis of Steyne—"The atrocious monster!" Forced to flee by insult; coward pursued revenge by taking child from her. Emmy received story with indignation at conduct of "miserable Rawdon" and "unprincipled Steyne." During separation scene, Emmy "retired altogether behind her pocket-handkerchief." Amelia offered: "She may have Payne's room...The poor creature, after all her sufferings...quite alone and absolutely forced to give lessons in singing to get her bread—and not have her here!"

## Georgy Meets Becky; Dinner Scene (Chapter 28)

Georgy came in from fetes for dinner-time and found four covers laid as usual; one place occupied by a lady instead of by Major Dobbin. "Hullo! where's Dob?" the young gentleman asked with his usual simplicity of language. Amelia said Major was dining out, kissed Georgy a great deal, put his hair off his forehead, introduced him to Mrs. Crawley. "This is my boy, Rebecca," Mrs. Osborne said—as much as to say—can the world produce anything like that? Becky looked at him with rapture and pressed his hand fondly. "Dear boy!" she said—"he is just like my--" Emotion choked her further utterance, but Amelia understood that Becky was thinking of her own blessed child. Company of her friend consoled Mrs. Crawley, and she ate a very good dinner.

During repast, she had occasion to speak several times, when Georgy eyed her and listened to her. At dessert Emmy was gone out to superintend further domestic arrangements; Jos was in his great chair dozing over Galignani; Georgy and new arrival sat close to each other—he had continued to look at her knowingly more than once, and at last he laid down the nutcrackers.

## Major Dobbin's Night of Anguish; Plan to Speak (Chapter 28)

Major had been advised in morning (before meeting with Rebecca) that Amelia should go to Court ball that night. There he should tell her his secret. He dressed in uniform, repaired to Court in hopes to see Mrs. Osborne. She never came. When he returned, all lights in Sedley tenement were put out. He could not see her till morning. "I don't know what sort of a night's rest he had with this frightful secret in bed with him."

## Amelia's Night of Reflection (Chapter 28)

She, too, had been awake all that night, thinking of a thing which had agitated her mind a hundred times before. A hundred times on point of yielding, she had shrunk back from sacrifice which she felt was too much for her. She couldn't, in spite of Dobbin's love and constancy and her own acknowledged regard, respect, and gratitude, accept him: "What are benefits, what is constancy, or merit? One curl of a girl's ringlet, one hair of a whisker, will turn the scale against them all in a minute. They did not weigh with Emmy more than with other women. She had tried them; wanted to make them pass; could not; and the pitiless little woman had found a pretext, and determined to be free."

## Major Dobbin's Confrontation and Final Break (Chapter 28)

Major encountered Rebecca and Amelia. Rebecca declared: "Yours is a very modest and convenient sort of calumny, Major Dobbin. You leave me under the weight of an accusation which, after all, is unsaid...My honour is as untouched as that of the bitterest enemy who ever maligned me...Let me go, Emmy. It is only to suppose that I have not met you, and I am no worse to-day than I was yesterday...Don't you remember the song we used to sing in old, dear old days? I have been wandering ever since then—a poor castaway, scorned for being miserable, and insulted because I am alone. Let me go: my stay here interferes with the plans of this gentleman."

**Dobbin's Final Speech and Rejection of Amelia (Chapter 28)**: William said sadly: "You don't mean that these words, uttered in a hurried moment, are to weigh against a whole life's devotion? I think that George's memory has not been injured by the way in which I have dealt with it, and if we are come to bandying reproaches, I at least merit none from his widow and the mother of his son."

He continued: "It is not that speech of yesterday which moves you. That is but the pretext, Amelia, or I have loved you and watched you for fifteen years in vain. Have I not learned in that time to read all your feelings and look into your thoughts? I know what your heart is capable of: it can cling faithfully to a recollection and cherish a fancy, but it can't feel such an attachment as mine deserves to mate with...No, you are not worthy of the love which I have devoted to you. I knew all along that the prize I had set my life on was not worth the winning...I will bargain no more: I withdraw...Good-bye, Amelia! I have watched your struggle. Let it end. We are both weary of it."

**Amelia's Shock and Loss**: Amelia stood scared and silent as William thus suddenly broke the chain by which she held him and declared his independence and superiority. He had placed himself at her feet so long that the poor little woman had been accustomed to trample upon him. "She didn't wish to marry him, but she wished to keep him. She wished to give him nothing, but that he should give her all. It is a bargain not unfrequently levied in love." With his departure, she loses her devoted follower.

## Key Character States
- **Amelia**: Has embraced Rebecca's false narrative completely; offended by Dobbin's allusions to past jealousy; rejected Dobbin's love by withholding herself, though not willing to lose his devotion; now abandoned by Major Dobbin after refusing him for fifteen years.
- **Major Dobbin**: Has broken definitively with Amelia; ended fifteen years of devoted service and hidden love; declared her unworthy of his attachment; departed, freeing himself from the relationship.
- **Rebecca**: Successfully manipulated Jos into believing her virtue; installed in Amelia's household; actively seducing Georgy with her presence; has displaced Dobbin from household and Amelia's affections.
- **Jos Sedley**: Convinced of Becky's virtue and misery; planning to help her settle respectably; resentful of Dobbin's superiority.
- **Georgy**: Met Becky; impressed by her; attentive to her at dinner.
- **Rawdon Crawley**: Separated permanently from Rebecca; financially settled on three hundred pounds per year with understanding she never trouble him again; transformed morally; governs Coventry Island.
